summary: Specifies the Binary Floor Control Protocol, used to manage joint or exclusive access to shared resources in a conference. Floor control complements conference setup, media control and policy protocols. It was standards-track and has been replaced by RFC 8855.

plainLanguage.summary: BFCP decides who has the floor in a conference, that is, who is allowed to send media at a given moment. A participant asks for the floor, a server grants or denies the request, and a moderator, called the chair, can overrule the server.

questions: how to manage who speaks in a conference
subtitle: How a conference decides who gets to speak, and who holds the floor when several people want it.

tldr.problem: In a conference with several people in it, someone has to decide who may send audio or video at any moment. Without a rule, people talk over each other.
tldr.mechanism: BFCP is a protocol between floor participants, floor chairs and a floor control server. A participant sends a FloorRequest, the server grants or denies it, and the chair can override the server's decisions.
tldr.outcome: The server also tells participants and chairs when a request is accepted, queued, granted or released, so everyone can see who has the floor. The document has been replaced by RFC 8855.

today: RFC 4582 was a Proposed Standard published in November 2006. It has been obsoleted by RFC 8855, which is the current Binary Floor Control Protocol. It was in turn updated by RFC 8996.

sections.title: What Floor Control Is For
sections.content:
Floor control is a means to manage joint or exclusive access to shared resources in a multiparty conferencing environment. Thereby floor control complements other functions, such as conference and media session setup, conference policy manipulation and media control, that are realized by other protocols.

BFCP is used between floor participants and floor control servers, and between floor chairs, that is moderators, and floor control servers. The RFC's own figure shows the three roles and the two directions of traffic: a floor participant sends a floor request to a floor control server, which replies with a granted or denied answer; a floor chair sends decisions about floor requests to the same server; and the server sends notifications about the status of a floor or a floor request back to both the participant and the chair.

BFCP provides a means for floor participants to send floor requests to floor control servers, for floor control servers to grant or deny requests to access a given resource from floor participants, for floor chairs to send floor control servers decisions regarding floor requests, and for floor control servers to keep floor participants and floor chairs informed about the status of a given floor or a given floor request.

The scope of floor control is not unlimited. The association of a given floor with a resource or a set of resources is out of scope, as are floor creation and termination, which are handled using the conference control protocol for manipulating the conference object. The consequence is that the floor control server needs to stay up to date on changes to the conference object, for example when a new floor is created.
sections.plainLanguage: Three parties are involved: the people who want to talk, the moderator, and the server that keeps the list. BFCP covers the requests and the answers; it does not create the floors or decide which streams a floor belongs to.

sections.title: What Is Outside BFCP
sections.content:
A client needs a set of data in order to establish a BFCP connection to a floor control server: the transport address of the server, the conference identifier and a user identifier. Clients can obtain this information in different ways, one of which is an SDP offer/answer exchange. Other mechanisms are described in the XCON framework.

Floors are associated with resources. A floor that controls who talks at a given time has a particular audio session as its associated resource, and the associations between floors and resources are part of the conference object. Floor participants and floor chairs need to know which resources are associated with which floors, and they can obtain this information by using different mechanisms such as an SDP offer/answer exchange. Floor participants perform SDP offer/answer exchanges with the conference focus of the conference, so the conference focus needs to obtain information about associations between floors and resources in order to provide it to a floor participant in that exchange.

The RFC is careful about the meaning of holding a floor. A participant whose floor request is granted has the right to use, in a certain way, the resource or resources associated with the floor that was requested. For example, the participant may have the right to send media over a particular audio stream. Nevertheless, holding a floor does not imply that others will not be able to use its associated resources at the same time, even if they do not have the right to do so. Determining which media participants can actually use the resources in the conference is discussed in the XCON Framework.
sections.plainLanguage: The floor is only a permission to use a resource. It does not by itself stop anyone else from sending media, and the mapping from floors to streams lives in the conference description, not in BFCP.

sections.title: The Three Parties and the Message Flow
sections.content:
BFCP messages use a TLV binary encoding and consist of a common header followed by a set of attributes. The common header contains, among other information, a 32-bit conference identifier. Floor participants, media participants and floor chairs are identified by 16-bit user identifiers. BFCP supports nested attributes, that is attributes that contain attributes, which are referred to as grouped attributes.

There are two types of transactions. Client-initiated transactions consist of a message from a client to the floor control server and a response from the server to the client; both messages carry the same Transaction ID in their common headers, so they can be related. Server-initiated transactions consist of a single message, whose Transaction ID is 0, from the floor control server to a client.

Floor participants request a floor by sending a FloorRequest message. BFCP supports third-party floor requests: the floor participant sending the request need not be colocated with the media participant that will get the floor once the request is granted. FloorRequest messages carry the identity of the requester in the User ID field of the common header, and the identity of the beneficiary, in third-party requests, in a BENEFICIARY-ID attribute. FloorRequest messages identify the floor or floors being requested by carrying their 16-bit floor identifiers in FLOOR-ID attributes. If a FloorRequest message carries more than one floor identifier, the server treats all the floor requests as an atomic package, so it either grants or denies all the floors in the message.

The server responds to FloorRequest messages with FloorRequestStatus messages, which carry the status of the floor request. The first FloorRequestStatus message is the response to the FloorRequest and therefore has the same Transaction ID; it also carries the Floor Request ID. Subsequent FloorRequestStatus messages related to the same floor request carry the same Floor Request ID, so the participant can associate them with the appropriate request. In the RFC's worked example the status of a request moves through Pending, then Accepted with a queue position of 1st, then Granted, and finally Released when the participant sends a FloorRelease message with the same Floor Request ID.
sections.plainLanguage: A request carries a transaction number and a request number. The server answers with the status, first pending, then accepted with a place in the queue, then granted, and later released when the holder gives it up.

sections.title: The Packet Format
sections.content:
BFCP packets consist of a 12-octet common header followed by attributes, and all protocol values MUST be sent in network byte order. The common header carries a 3-bit version field which MUST be set to 1, a 5-bit reserved field which SHOULD be set to zero by the sender and MUST be ignored by the receiver, an 8-bit primitive field identifying the main purpose of the message, a 16-bit payload length field giving the length of the message in 4-octet units excluding the common header, a 32-bit conference identifier, a 16-bit transaction identifier used to match a given message with its response, and a 16-bit user identifier that uniquely identifies a participant within a conference.

Thirteen primitives are defined. FloorRequest and FloorRelease travel from participant to server. FloorRequestQuery, UserQuery and FloorQuery travel from participant or chair to server. FloorRequestStatus, UserStatus and FloorStatus travel back from the server. ChairAction travels from chair to server and ChairActionAck comes back. Hello and HelloAck are exchanged in both directions, and Error comes from the server.

Attributes are encoded in TLV format and are 32-bit aligned. Each attribute has a 7-bit type, an M bit, an 8-bit length, and contents. The M bit, known as the Mandatory bit, indicates whether support of the attribute is required: if an unrecognized attribute with the M bit set is received, the message is rejected. The M bit is significant for extension attributes defined in other documents only, since all attributes specified in this document MUST be understood by the receiver. The attribute formats are Unsigned16, OctetString16, OctetString and Grouped, the last meaning a sequence of attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: Every BFCP packet has a fixed 12-byte header naming the version, the kind of message, the conference, the transaction and the user, followed by a list of typed attributes that may themselves contain further attributes.

sections.title: Transport, Security and Transactions
sections.content:
BFCP entities exchange BFCP messages using TCP connections, and since TCP provides an in-order reliable delivery of a stream of bytes, message framing is implemented in the application layer, using TLV-encoded attributes. A client MUST NOT use more than one TCP connection to communicate with a given floor control server within a conference, although if the same physical box handles different clients, identified by different User IDs, a separate connection per client is allowed. If a BFCP entity receives data from TCP that cannot be parsed, it MUST close the TCP connection, and the connection SHOULD be reestablished. When the server detects that the connection towards one of the floor participants is lost, it is RECOMMENDED that it keep the pending floor requests rather than cancel them while the connection is reestablished.

BFCP relies on lower-layer security mechanisms to provide replay and integrity protection and confidentiality. Floor control servers and clients MUST support TLS, and at a minimum the TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA ciphersuite. Which party acts as the TLS server depends on how the underlying TCP connection is established: when it is established using an SDP offer/answer exchange, the answerer always acts as the TLS server.

For transactions, a client starting a client-initiated transaction MUST set the Conference ID in the common header to the conference identifier it obtained previously, and MUST set the Transaction ID to a number different from 0 that must not be reused in another message until a response has been received. A server sending a response within a client-initiated transaction MUST copy the Conference ID, the Transaction ID and the User ID from the request into the response, and server-initiated transactions MUST contain a Transaction ID equal to 0.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages travel over TCP, protected by TLS so that only the two ends can read them. Each request carries a number that the server copies into the reply, so a client can tell which reply belongs to which request.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
BFCP uses TLS to provide mutual authentication between clients and servers, and TLS also provides replay and integrity protection and confidentiality. It is RECOMMENDED that TLS with non-null encryption always be used. BFCP entities MAY use other security mechanisms as long as they provide similar security properties.

The RFC then analyses the main threats. An attacker may attempt to impersonate a client, a floor participant or a floor chair, in order to generate forged floor requests or to grant or deny existing floor requests. Client impersonation is avoided by having servers only accept BFCP messages over authenticated TLS connections, since the server assumes that attackers cannot hijack the TLS connection and therefore that messages over it come from the client that was initially authenticated. An attacker may also attempt to impersonate a floor control server, which would let them make clients think they hold a particular floor so that they would try to access a resource without legitimate rights; server impersonation is avoided by having clients only accept messages over authenticated TLS connections.

Attackers may attempt to modify messages exchanged by a client and a floor control server, which the integrity protection provided by TLS connections prevents. They may attempt to fetch a valid message sent by a client and replay it over a connection between the attacker and the server; this is prevented by having floor control servers check that messages arriving over a given authenticated TLS connection use an authorized user ID, that is, a user ID that the user that established the connection is allowed to use. Attackers may attempt to pick messages from the network to get access to confidential information between the server and a client, such as why a floor request was denied, which TLS confidentiality prevents.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything rests on TLS: it proves who each end is, keeps the messages unaltered, and stops an outsider reading why a request was turned down. The server also checks that a user ID arriving on a connection is one that connection is allowed to use.

messages.label: FLOORREQUEST
messages.note: Carries the Transaction ID, the User ID and a FLOOR-ID.

messages.label: FLOORREQUESTSTATUS: PENDING
messages.note: The reply to the request, carrying a new Floor Request ID.

messages.label: FLOORREQUESTSTATUS: ACCEPTED
messages.note: A server-initiated notification giving the queue position.

messages.label: FLOORREQUESTSTATUS: GRANTED
messages.note: The floor is now held by the participant.

messages.label: FLOORRELEASE
messages.note: Gives the floor up, quoting the Floor Request ID.

fields.name: Ver
fields.desc: The version field; must be set to 1.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Should be set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

fields.name: Primitive
fields.desc: Identifies the main purpose of the message.

fields.name: Payload Length
fields.desc: Length of the message in 4-octet units, excluding the common header.

fields.name: Conference ID
fields.desc: Identifies the conference the message belongs to.

fields.name: Transaction ID
fields.desc: Matches a message with its response; 0 in server-initiated transactions.

fields.name: User ID
fields.desc: Uniquely identifies a participant within a conference.

viz.caption: THE BFCP PRIMITIVES AND WHO SENDS THEM

items.label: FloorRequest
items.desc: Participant to server: asks for one or more floors.

items.label: FloorRelease
items.desc: Participant to server: gives a floor back.

items.label: FloorRequestQuery
items.desc: Participant or chair to server: asks about a request.

items.label: FloorRequestStatus
items.desc: Server to participant or chair: the status of a request.

items.label: ChairAction
items.desc: Chair to server: a decision about a floor request.

items.label: Error
items.desc: Server to participant or chair: something went wrong.
